html_en:
OpenAI slashes prices dramatically while the industry grapples with two converging anxieties: agents that escape sandboxes and the infrastructural weight of building AI that actually works in the physical world.

💸 The Price War Accelerates

The biggest news of the day came from Sam Altman, who announced sweeping cuts across OpenAI's model lineup:

"Major price cuts today: 80% drop for GPT-5.6 Luna, now $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output. 20% drop for GPT-5.6 Terra, to $2/$12. GPT-5.6 Sol gets Fast mode in the API, up to 2.5x the speed for 2x the price, same intelligence." — @sama

The strategic intent is clear. In a separate post, Altman added simply: "we want to offer the best price/intelligence tradeoff at every level." An 80% price drop on a frontier-adjacent model isn't a tweak — it's a land grab.

Box CEO Aaron Levie offered the clearest framework for why this dynamic is structural, not promotional:

"The general trend we should expect is that frontier AI models will continue to become more capable, and will look very expensive because the tasks that they can take on are more advanced. Then, shortly after, AI models will get more efficient or competition will drive more aggressive pricing dynamics… This cycle will continue over and over again, which ultimately leads to tasks becoming cheaper on a like for like basis." — @levie

🏗️ The Hidden Infrastructure Tax of Pretraining

One of the more quietly viral observations of the day came from Shawn Wang (@swyx), who articulated something that feels obvious in retrospect but rarely gets said plainly:

"If you prioritize pretrain data quality enough that CommonCrawl isn't good enough for you, you have to build a Whole Web scraper anyway, and if you wanna keep it current, you have to have indexing, and pretty soon you find yourself having built a total private low-frequency clone of Google as a SIDE PROJECT of pretraining, that you can then also reuse for the agent side inference." — @swyx

This isn't just an interesting observation about lab economics — it explains why search and AI are converging at the infrastructure level, not just the product level. The labs aren't building search as a feature. They're building it because they have to. And once built, it becomes a competitive moat they have every incentive to keep private.

Swyx also floated a cheeky corollary: if you can distill models, you can distill agent harnesses too — suggesting the same compression techniques reshaping model economics might soon apply to the scaffolding around them.

🔐 Agents in the Wild: The Sandbox Problem

The week's ongoing conversation about AI agents escaping containment prompted sharp takes from multiple corners. Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, which has been running sandboxes since 2016, offered the most grounded perspective:

"With all the 'AI escaping sandbox' it's easy to think 'wow AI so scary,' but most AI companies, and recent 'sandbox providers' are making very basic mistakes… Main advice: Assume zero-days exist — because they do — and think in layers of protection in a zero-trust framework." — @amasad

Levie reframed the safety conversation away from AI alignment and toward enterprise IT hardening:

"The takeaway from this incident should not be that AI is scary. It should be that getting security right is incredibly important in the era of agents. Given the right tools and task, agents will do whatever it takes to get the job done, assuming enough compute. Thus, a misconfigured system — or something you thought was locked down but wasn't — will become a risk vector." — @levie

Dan Shipper was more wry: "So call me crazy but I feel like we could solve this by just not prompting the models to do cyber crime."

🚛 The Biggest AI Deployment Nobody's Talking About

While the discourse fixates on chatbots and coding agents, Matt Turck sat down with Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas for what might be the most grounding conversation of the week. Samsara — a $20B public company — covers 99% of US roads daily, processes 25 trillion data points a year, and claims to have helped prevent 380,000 road accidents in the last year alone.

"These are not the tokens you're gonna find online. Like, you can't crawl Reddit and find out about what happened on a construction site." — Sanjit Biswas, The MAD Podcast

Biswas's explanation of why physical AI lagged digital AI is worth sitting with:

"It makes complete sense where all of this AI wave has started, which is in the digital world. We had all the bits. We had petabytes of data to reason over… The physical world is much messier, and there's also a hardware component to it. This stuff has to hold up in the environment. It's got to relay the data over unreliable networks. It has to be deployed to the front lines, and that requires a lot of sort of messy work." — Sanjit Biswas

Watch/Listen: The Biggest AI Deployment Nobody Talks About | The MAD Podcast

⚡ Quick Sparks

Grok meets Vercel: Guillermo Rauch announced that Grok Build apps are now backed by Vercel hosting and CDN infrastructure — anyone can prompt Grok, hit publish, and ship to a billion users. Vercel also shaved up to 7 seconds off CLI-to-live-URL deploy times, which matters more as autonomous software factories become real.

The GCC LLM ban: Peter Steinberger (@steipete) flagged that GCC is now blanket-rejecting LLM-generated code contributions — raising the obvious question of how they'd ever prove it.

Enterprise AI onboarding, solved: Zara Zhang shared the most practical advice of the day for anyone trying to get non-technical colleagues actually using AI tools: "Run an install party. Everyone brings a laptop & you install the agents right there on their machines & get them to complete a meaningful task on the spot. Skip the abstract talk. The setup is 80% the barrier."

A sign of better models: Finally, Thomas Sottiaux offered a quietly haunting observation that's been circulating widely: "The day we develop really good models. There will be signs. Reliability increasing despite load going up and up. Sudden efficiency gains. Things getting faster. Resets." Worth bookmarking for when those signs start appearing.
html_zh:
今天AI圈有两条主线并行推进：OpenAI宣布大幅降价，将智能的获取成本再次压低；与此同时，一场关于AI安全边界的讨论正在发酵——从沙盒逃逸事件到企业环境加固，行业正在直面"能力越强、风险越大"的现实。

💸 OpenAI大幅降价，价格战进入新阶段

今天最受瞩目的消息来自 Sam Altman。OpenAI宣布对多款模型进行大幅降价：

GPT-5.6 Luna 降价 80%，每百万输入token仅需 $0.20，输出 $1.20；GPT-5.6 Terra 降价 20%，至 $2/$12；GPT-5.6 Sol 则在 API 中新增快速模式，速度最高提升2.5倍。
— @sama

Altman 随后补充了这一战略的核心逻辑：

"我们希望在每一个层级都提供最佳的价格/智能比。"
— @sama

Aaron Levie 对这一趋势给出了更宏观的解读：AI成本的下降是推动整个经济体AI普及的最关键因素之一。他预测，这将形成一个持续循环——前沿模型能力增强、价格先升后降、任务单价不断走低，最终让更多场景和企业用得起AI。这不是一次性的价格调整，而是行业结构性演变的缩影。

🔐 沙盒逃逸与安全边界：能力越强，风险越真实

最近一起AI"逃脱沙盒"事件在圈内引发了热烈讨论。Amjad Masad（Replit CEO）从一家从2016年起就在运营沙盒、被无数黑客和国家级攻击者盯上的公司角度，给出了最务实的建议：

"假设零日漏洞是存在的——因为它确实存在——并以零信任框架构建多层防护。"
— @amasad

Levie 则从企业视角补充道：这类事件的核心教训不是"AI很可怕"，而是系统配置错误、环境未加固才是真正的风险向量。Dan Shipper 的反应则更加直白：

"也许我们可以不要在提示词里让模型去做网络犯罪？"
— @danshipper

这场讨论提醒我们：随着Agent能力的持续提升，安全问题不再只是研究院里的思想实验，而是每一个部署AI系统的工程师和企业都必须面对的现实工作。

🏗️ 物理AI：最大的AI部署，你可能从未听说过

Matt Turck 在 MAD Podcast 中与 Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas 的对话，揭示了一个被科技媒体严重低估的AI应用场景。Watch/Listen: The Biggest AI Deployment Nobody Talks About | Samsara CEO Sanjit Biswas

Samsara 每天覆盖美国99%的道路，积累了25万亿个数据点，据称在过去一年帮助预防了约38万起交通事故。Biswas 解释了物理AI为何如此难啃：

"这些token你在网上找不到。你没办法爬Reddit去了解一个建筑工地上发生了什么。物理世界要混乱得多，还有硬件这个维度。这些设备必须在恶劣环境中运行，通过不稳定的网络传输数据，还需要部署到一线，让数以百万计的工人真正用起来。"
— Sanjit Biswas

他们讨论的核心洞察是：过去二十年，物理行业的数字化只做到了"报告"层面——把数据汇成表格让人去读。真正的突破在于，AI现在能够推理这些数据、主动给出行动建议，甚至直接代替人执行操作。物理AI的护城河，或许正是这些永远无法被公开爬取的"现实世界token"。

🕸️ 预训练数据与搜索引擎的隐秘融合

swyx 分享了一个他认为"事后看来显而易见"的顿悟时刻，道出了大模型训练背后一个鲜少被公开讨论的逻辑：

"如果你对预训练数据质量要求极高，高到CommonCrawl都不够用，你就必须自己造一个完整的网络爬虫。如果你还想保持数据的时效性，你就得做索引。很快你会发现，你顺手造了一个私有的低频版Google——只是作为预训练的副产品。而这套东西，之后又可以直接复用到推理侧的Agent搜索上。"
— @swyx

这一视角解释了为什么各大实验室都在悄悄构建自己的第一方搜索能力，而非依赖第三方：这既是竞争优势，也是防止"AEO拟态攻击"（AI引擎优化伪装）的必要手段。他还顺带提了一个有些无奈的观察：如果大家把涌入各路AI项目的钱都捐给 Wayback Machine，或许能省去大量重复工作和爬虫流量。

⚡ 工具与信号：本周值得留意的几件小事

Grok × Vercel： Guillermo Rauch 宣布 Grok Build 应用（*.grok.me）已由 Vercel 提供托管和CDN基础设施支撑。任何人只需用自然语言提示 @grok，点击"发布"，即可将应用推送给1个用户或10亿用户。与此同时，Vercel CLI 到上线的端到端流程已缩短最多约7秒。

AI推广最佳实践： @zarazhangrui 给出了一个简洁有效的非技术团队AI培训建议：举办"安装派对"——把所有人聚在一起，当场在各自电脑上装好Agent，完成一个有意义的任务。"设置本身占据了80%的障碍。"

好消息预兆： 一条来自 @thsottiaux 的推文获得了超4000个点赞——他描述了真正强大的AI模型出现时，系统层面可能会出现的信号：可靠性在高负载下不降反升、效率突然跃升、速度加快、系统重置。这像是一位工程师从内部视角写下的"技术奇点预警清单"，耐人寻味。
